problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3-{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2}+4t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-{t}^{2})=-2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4t)=2t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{{(-2t)}^{2}+{(2t+4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{16(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\cdot 4\cdot \sqrt{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
